notes.meaning: Achan secretly took some of the plunder from Jericho that God had commanded to be completely destroyed. Even though only one person committed the theft, God held the whole community accountable for breaking covenant trust. Because the nation was bound together as one body before God, His anger burned against all the people of Israel.

Joshua sent scouts from Jericho to inspect Ai, a smaller town located near Bethel in the hill country. This was a sensible military step to learn the approaches and avoid falling into an ambush. Yet Joshua moved forward with his own plans without first asking the Lord for guidance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists are uncertain whether Ai was an inhabited town during this period, leading some to suggest it was an outpost of Bethel.

notes.meaning: When the scouts returned, they told Joshua that only two or three thousand soldiers were needed because Ai had few defenders. They wanted to spare the rest of the army a hard march up the steep hills. Their report made Israel overconfident, forgetting that numbers mean nothing without God's help.

About three thousand Israelite soldiers marched up the mountain to attack Ai, but they fled almost immediately from the town's defenders. Because God had withdrawn His favor, the soldiers lost their courage before the fight even gained momentum. This painful retreat showed that Israel had no strength of their own when God was not with them.

The men of Ai chased the Israelites down the rocky slopes as far as the stone quarries and killed about thirty-six soldiers. Though the loss of life was small for an army, the shock of defeat shattered Israel's confidence. The people panicked, and their courage melted away like water.

Joshua and the elders of Israel tore their clothes, put dust on their heads, and lay face down before the ark of the Lord until evening. These actions were traditional signs of deep grief and humble repentance. Joshua knew this defeat was not bad luck in battle, but a sign that God had turned away from them.

Joshua cried out in confusion, asking why God had brought them across the Jordan only to let the Amorites wipe them out. He even blurted out that they should have remained on the other side of the river. His words showed human weakness and fear, yet he took his honest anguish straight to the Lord.

Joshua lamented that he had no answer to give now that Israel had run from their enemies. God had promised them total victory in the land, so running away seemed to contradict everything Joshua had declared. He grieved deeply over the public disgrace brought upon the Lord's people.

Joshua feared that once the Canaanites and other nations heard about the retreat, they would surround Israel and destroy them. Most of all, he was concerned for God's honor, asking what would become of the Lord's great name if His people perished. Joshua made God's glory and reputation the main plea of his prayer.

The Lord told Joshua to get up off his face and stop lying on the ground. Mourning had its place, but the time for passive weeping was over because serious work had to be done. Joshua needed to rise and take direct steps to uncover and remove the sin in the camp.

God declared that Israel had sinned and broken the covenant by taking items devoted to destruction. The offender had stolen what belonged to the Lord, lied to conceal it, and hidden the plunder among his own belongings. Even though one man stole the goods, God viewed the whole nation as tainted by the crime.

The Lord explained that the Israelites could not stand before their enemies because they had made themselves subject to the same curse of destruction. He warned that He would not stay with them unless they destroyed the devoted things from their midst. Unconfessed sin robs God's people of His protection and power.

God told Joshua to summon the people to consecrate themselves for the next morning. Consecration meant ceremonial washing and preparing their hearts to meet God's holy inspection. Announcing the investigation a day early also gave the guilty person time to confess voluntarily.

The Lord directed that the people appear before Him tribe by tribe, clan by clan, family by family, and finally man by man. God Himself would single out the guilty party at each step, likely through the casting of lots before the sanctuary. This careful search showed that God knows every secret deed and will judge with perfect accuracy.

God ordered that whoever was caught with the devoted goods must be burned with fire along with everything he owned. This severe penalty answered the offender's crime of breaking God's covenant and bringing disgraceful folly upon Israel. Utterly burning the stolen goods and the culprit's possessions was required to purge the curse completely.

Joshua got up early the next morning to obey the Lord without delay and presented Israel tribe by tribe. When the selection was made before the Lord, the tribe of Judah was taken. Joshua's prompt obedience showed his urgent desire to remove the curse and restore God's blessing.

Next, the clans of Judah were brought forward, and the clan of the Zerahites was singled out. Joshua then had the family units of that clan step up, and the household of Zabdi was chosen. The circle of investigation grew smaller step by step, showing the unerring hand of God at work.

Joshua brought Zabdi's household forward man by man, and Achan was finally chosen. Achan had watched the selection draw closer and closer to him, yet his hardened heart had kept him from stepping forward on his own. Secret sins cannot stay hidden forever when God calls a person to account.

Joshua spoke gently to Achan, calling him 'my son' and urging him to give glory to the Lord by confessing the whole truth. Giving glory to God meant admitting that the Lord sees all things and that His judgment is entirely righteous. Joshua showed a fatherly spirit toward the sinner while remaining firm in upholding God's justice.

Achan answered Joshua and openly admitted that he had sinned against the Lord, the God of Israel. Stripped of any chance to deny the truth, he made no excuses and confessed exactly what he had done. He acknowledged that his crime was not just against the camp, but against the God who had chosen them.

Achan explained how his sin unfolded: he saw a beautiful Babylonian robe, two hundred silver coins, and a heavy bar of gold, coveted them, and took them. He then dug a hole inside his tent and buried the treasures in the dirt, placing the silver beneath the rest. His story reveals the dangerous path of sin, which starts with looking, turns into greed, and ends in wrongful action.

Joshua sent messengers who ran immediately to Achan's tent to verify his confession. They found the stolen items buried in the ground inside the tent, with the silver hidden underneath, exactly as Achan had confessed. The messengers ran quickly because everyone was eager to remove the curse and restore peace with God.

The messengers pulled the hidden items from the tent and brought them to Joshua and the gathered Israelites. They laid everything out before the Lord in front of the sanctuary as physical proof of the crime. This public display confirmed that the stolen goods were God's property and vindicated His judgment against the camp.

Joshua and all the people took Achan, the stolen goods, his family, his livestock, and all his belongings to the Valley of Achor. The execution had to be held outside the camp so the dwelling place of the community would not remain defiled by the curse. Everything tied to Achan's household was brought out to completely remove the contamination from Israel.

Joshua asked Achan why he had brought trouble on Israel and declared that the Lord would bring trouble on him that day. The whole assembly then stoned Achan and burned the remains with fire, carrying out God's sentence. By participating together, the people demonstrated their total rejection of the sin and their desire to turn away God's anger.

differ.view: Some hold that only Achan was put to death, while his children were brought out only to watch the punishment and take warning, because the law forbade killing children for their parents' sins.
Many hold that Achan's children were executed with him because they likely helped conceal the stolen goods in the tent and shared in the guilt of the devoted things.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that Achan was executed along with his children and herds under the total ban placed upon Jericho.

notes.meaning: The Israelites raised a large heap of stones over Achan as a lasting monument and warning to future generations. Once the sin was judged and removed, the Lord turned from His fierce anger against the nation. The place was named the Valley of Achor, meaning 'trouble,' marking the spot where Israel's trouble was purged and hope was restored.
